headline: Curaleaf wins US patent for water-based cannabinoid extraction
dek: The USPTO granted Curaleaf patent 12,806,240 on 24 November for extracting cannabinoids with alkaline water; a version already makes its Florida ACE oil.
key_points: The US Patent and Trademark Office issued patent 12,806,240, 'Aqueous extraction of cannabinoids', to Curaleaf on 24 November, with 11 claims.
The core claim covers circulating an alkaline water solution between two stirred-tank reactors, one holding cannabis and one holding a resin that captures the cannabinoids.
A Curaleaf spokesperson told The Marijuana Herald that an updated version of the process is used to make the company's ACE vape oil in Florida.
The patent's background pitches the method as an alternative to hydrocarbon, alcohol and supercritical CO2 extraction, which it says are costly and carry safety risks.
body: Curaleaf has been granted a US patent for extracting cannabinoids from cannabis using water rather than solvents or pressurised gas. The US Patent and Trademark Office issued patent number 12,806,240, titled 'Aqueous extraction of cannabinoids', on 24 November, according to the Official Gazette. The patent is assigned to Curaleaf, Inc., names Andrew Lux and Robert Scott Winnicki as inventors and contains 11 claims.

The process is not just on paper. A Curaleaf spokesperson told The Marijuana Herald that the company uses an updated version of the method to make its ACE oil in Florida. ACE stands for aqueous cannabinoid extraction.

The first claim, as printed in the Gazette, describes a continuous extraction method. An aqueous base solution, essentially alkaline water, is circulated between two stirred-tank reactors. The first holds cannabis plant material; the second holds a hydrophobic chromatography resin. As the solution circulates, cannabinoids move out of the plant into the water and then bind to the resin, from which they can be recovered.

The published application, filed on 27 February 2024 and made public in August 2024, fills in the detail. It describes base solutions such as sodium or potassium hydroxide at concentrations of roughly 0.1 to 0.6 molar, with 0.3 molar given as one example, and a plant-to-solution ratio of 1:2 to 1:20 by weight to volume. Cannabinoids bound to the resin can then be washed out into ethanol and purified further by distillation, evaporation, chromatography or acid precipitation. A second route in the application precipitates cannabinoids directly out of the alkaline extract by adding acid.

According to The Marijuana Herald, the application says the method can extract THC, CBD, CBG and CBN and can reach above 99% total cannabinoid purity, or above 98% for individual cannabinoids. The application also describes the approach as suitable for small and large operations.

Most cannabis extraction today relies on hydrocarbons such as butane and propane, on ethanol, or on supercritical CO2. The patent's own background section argues that those reagents are costly and create safety risks, and that operators may need explosion-proof equipment and large solvent-recycling systems to manage them. A water-based first stage, if it works at scale, would sidestep much of that.

Curaleaf's pitch to consumers is purity. The spokesperson told the Herald that the alkaline-water method leaves behind most of the plant by-products that persist in typical vape oils, and described ACE oil as purer and smoother than regular vape oil. The company sells it with either live cannabis-derived or botanical terpenes. Those are the company's claims; the patent itself makes no statements about product quality or safety for consumers.
> Curaleaf is turning a lab process into a moat. Whether it matters depends on how many rivals were heading down the same path.
## What a patent does and does not do

A granted patent gives Curaleaf the right to stop others from using the claimed method in the United States for the patent's term, subject to challenge. Its reach is set by the 11 claims, not by the broader description in the application, so competitors using other water-based approaches may fall outside it. The grant shows the patent office will protect a cannabis extraction method even while cannabis remains federally controlled; the harder question is enforcement in an industry where much manufacturing happens inside single-state licences.

For Curaleaf, the patent arrives in a busy month. The company opened its 82nd Florida dispensary, as we reported on 24 November, and its hostile offer for Aurora Cannabis is due to lapse on 4 December unless extended, ahead of the 23 December shareholder votes on Aurora's rival merger with Organigram, as we reported on 26 November. A proprietary extraction method is a small piece of that picture, but it is the kind of intellectual property multistate operators have used to differentiate products in crowded vape aisles.

Watch whether Curaleaf extends ACE products beyond Florida, and whether it licenses the method to other operators or asserts the patent against them. Watch also for any challenge to the patent, and for independent lab data on residual impurities in ACE oil compared with conventional distillate, which would test the company's purity claims.
